findings.text: The opening paragraph says what Athena is in one plain sentence. A newcomer can name the product without scrolling.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository.

findings.text: This is Athena's own site, but almost the whole page is about another project, firstmate. Athena gets about three sentences. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to work out that the rest of the page is a sample of its output, not documentation about Athena.
The page says why the study exists, but never says why a newcomer should care about Athena: who it is for, or what problem it solves for them. The demo only proves traceability.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The page promises these features, but nothing on it shows them. No checker model, cost record or request reading appears, so a newcomer has to take the headline features on trust.
findings.source: It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: There is a clear next-step link near the top and a Next steps section. But the install step gives no clone command, no prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or AI model access) and no hint of what `athena ask` will do to a repository. A newcomer would have to leave the page to start.
findings.source: Next steps — "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The firstmate sections assume a lot of background: exit codes, places-held, pending-close records, captain calls. A newcomer gets lost quickly. The 'Start here' section and the glossary help, but the transition cards are written for someone already studying firstmate's internals.
findings.source: Transitions — "Every worker place is held, so the spawn is deferred with exit 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: The same terms (yolo, red, green, in scope) are defined in full both in 'Words used first' and in the Glossary, and restated again in the bullets and cards. This makes a long page longer without adding anything.
findings.source: Start here — "Words used first" and Glossary entries for yolo, red, green

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to exact lines at a pinned commit. This is a convincing, checkable demonstration of what the page says Athena can do.
findings.source: Claims and sources — e.g. "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197" links at the pinned commit

findings.text: It is good that the page admits the study's limits. But a note about an earlier draft missing paths is internal process detail, and it may lower a newcomer's confidence instead of informing them.
findings.source: Limits of this study — f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"

findings.text: This section doesn't say which repository the `studies/` folder belongs to, so a newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: About this page — "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
